_comment: Adaptive exercise bank. Deterministic exercises (predict-output, find-a-bug, complete-code, write-a-function, modify-code, solve-without-AI, compare-implementations) carry 'expected_stdout' and are graded by compiling and running the learner's code. Free-form exercises (explain-code) carry a 'rubric' and are graded interpretively by AI, which the UI labels as such. 'novel': true marks an unfamiliar variation as opposed to the worked example. core/exercises.py validates this file on load.

exercises.title: Where does execution begin?
exercises.prompt: This program is missing a line. Predict what it prints as written, then fix it so it prints the message.

exercises.title: The missing semicolon
exercises.prompt: This should print two numbers but does not compile. Find the bug.

exercises.title: Explain the entry point
exercises.prompt: In your own words, explain what int main() does and what its return value means to the operating system. Do not repeat this page back to me; say what you think it is for.
rubric: mentions it is the entry point the OS calls
mentions the return value is an exit status
mentions 0 conventionally means success

exercises.title: Shadowing in a nested block
exercises.prompt: Two variables share a name. Predict the output.

exercises.title: Assigning to a const
exercises.prompt: This does not compile. Make it compile and still print 3.14159.

exercises.title: Swap two variables
exercises.prompt: Write a function void swap_values(int& a, int& b) that swaps the two variables the caller owns. main must end up printing '1 2' starting from a=2, b=1.

exercises.title: The integer division trap
exercises.prompt: Both expressions divide. Predict both lines exactly.

exercises.title: Wrong average
exercises.prompt: The average is printed as 0 but should be 2.5. Find and fix the cause.
Explain, in your own words, why total / count gives 2 instead of 2.5 here. Explain the underlying representation rather than just stating the result.
rubric: mentions integer division or truncation
mentions the fractional part is discarded
mentions that a double operand would be needed

exercises.title: The leftover newline
exercises.prompt: Read carefully: name is read with >> and the rest with getline. Predict the output for input 'Ada' then a blank line.

exercises.title: Empty full name
exercises.prompt: For input 'Ada Lovelace' this prints an empty surname. Fix it so it prints 'Lovelace'.

exercises.title: Validated integer reader
exercises.prompt: Without asking the tutor, write the loop that reads ints until the user enters 0, then prints how many were read. Run it with input '3 7 0' and it must print '2'.

exercises.title: Precedence and parentheses
exercises.prompt: Predict both lines.

exercises.title: Assignment used as a condition
exercises.prompt: This always runs and never prints 'nope'. Make it behave correctly so it prints 'nope'.

exercises.title: Modulo with negatives
exercises.prompt: Predict the output of both lines exactly, including signs.

exercises.title: The chain that matches everything
exercises.prompt: Every score becomes an A. Reorder the chain so 85 gives B and 92 gives A.

exercises.title: Exact float comparison
exercises.prompt: This never prints 'equal'. Make it print 'equal' using a sensible tolerance.
Explain why score 95 does not produce grade B here, and state the general rule you would follow when ordering such a chain.
rubric: mentions only the first true branch runs
mentions ordering from most specific to least
mentions the tests should be ordered highest threshold first

exercises.title: One number too many
exercises.prompt: It prints 6 instead of 5. Fix it.

exercises.title: The loop that never ends
exercises.prompt: This hangs. Make it count down and stop at zero.

exercises.title: Countdown from n
exercises.prompt: Write void countdown(int n) that prints n down to 1 separated by spaces, then a newline, and prints nothing when n <= 1.

exercises.title: Missing return
exercises.prompt: The program prints nothing useful. Make it print '7'.

exercises.title: The change that vanishes
exercises.prompt: The function is called but nothing changes. Fix it so it prints '11'.
Explain why n is unchanged after this call, and say what you would change about the parameter and why you would prefer that.
exercises.code:
void increment(int x) { x = x + 1; }
int main() { int n = 10; increment(n); /* n is still 10 */ }
rubric: mentions the parameter is a copy
mentions changing a copy cannot affect the caller
mentions passing by reference as the fix

exercises.title: Indexing past the end
exercises.prompt: This reads out of bounds. Fix it so it prints the sum of all four numbers, 10.

exercises.title: Find the largest
exercises.prompt: Write int find_max(const std::vector<int>& values) returning the largest element, and 0 for an empty vector. It must print 92 for the given input.
Explain what this loop prints, and why. Then say what would happen if the condition were changed to i <= 3 and why C++ would not stop you.
exercises.code:
int nums[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) std::cout << nums[i];
rubric: mentions it prints all four values in order
mentions indexing starts at zero so the last index is 3
mentions C++ does not bounds-check arrays at runtime

exercises.prompt: Explain what this prints and why, then say what would go wrong if the string were empty.
rubric: mentions size is 5
mentions s[size()-1] is the last character
mentions an empty string would underflow or read out of range

exercises.title: Count the vowels
exercises.prompt: Write int count_vowels(const std::string& text) that counts a, e, i, o, u case-insensitively. For 'Hello World' it must print 3.

exercises.title: Dereferencing nothing
exercises.prompt: This crashes. Make it print 'safe' when the pointer is null.

exercises.title: Testing an address against null
exercises.prompt: Predict both lines exactly. One of them is a surprise.
Explain what &value and *address each produce, and explain what happens to the original variable when it is written through the pointer.
rubric: mentions &value gives the address
mentions *address dereferences to the value
mentions writing through it changes the original variable

exercises.title: The reference that is not one
exercises.prompt: This does not compile, and should not. Replace the bad line so the program prints 5.
Explain what happens to the original variable when alias is assigned to, and explain why that is different from what would happen with a pointer.
rubric: mentions alias is an alias for first
mentions first now holds 2
mentions the reference is not reseated, unlike a pointer

exercises.title: The forgotten delete
exercises.prompt: This leaks. Fix it so the value is printed and no allocation is left dangling.

exercises.title: Freeing twice
exercises.prompt: This crashes because of a double free. Make it print 7 and free the memory exactly once.
Explain why risky_operation() throwing does not leak the file handle here, and say what the general rule is.
rubric: mentions the destructor runs during stack unwinding
mentions RAII
mentions the file is closed even on the exception path

exercises.title: Dot where you need an arrow
exercises.prompt: This does not compile because of the member access. Fix it so it prints 10.
Using the provided struct Point, write double distance_squared(const Point& a, const Point& b). For (0,0) and (3,4) it must print 25.

exercises.title: The read-only method that is not
exercises.prompt: This does not compile on a const object. Fix it so it prints 12.
Write a class Counter with a private int value_ initialised to 0, an increment() method, and int value() const. main must print 2.

exercises.title: Constructing an invalid object
exercises.prompt: The constructor accepts a negative balance. Make it reject it and print 'rejected'.
Explain the difference between initialising in the initialisation list versus assigning in the constructor body, and give one situation where only the list works.
rubric: mentions the list initialises directly
mentions the body default-constructs then overwrites
mentions const or reference members that cannot be assigned

exercises.title: The unchecked open
exercises.prompt: For a missing file this silently does nothing. Make it print 'missing'.

exercises.title: Truncate versus append
exercises.prompt: Before running, the file contains 'old\n'. Predict the file contents after this program runs.

exercises.title: The unreachable handler
exercises.prompt: The specific handler never runs because the broad one is first. Fix the order so it prints 'specific'.
Explain why the file still gets closed when risky_operation() throws, and say why you would not normally use catch(...) to close it manually.
rubric: mentions the destructor runs during unwinding
mentions RAII
mentions catch(...) would hide real errors

exercises.prompt: Two versions sum 1..n. Run both, then explain in your own words which one you would keep and why.
rubric: states both produce the same result
gives a reason grounded in readability or intent
mentions off-by-one risk in whichever is riskier

exercises.title: Rewrite a for loop as a while
exercises.prompt: Rewrite this for loop as a while loop that produces identical output, then run it to prove it.

exercises.title: Avoid the copy
exercises.prompt: Change the signature so the string is not copied on every call, without changing the output.

exercises.title: Complete the even test
exercises.prompt: Finish the function so it returns true for even numbers. The body is missing.

exercises.title: Complete the array sum
exercises.prompt: Fill in the loop so the total of the array is computed and printed as 55.
Run both versions, confirm they agree, then explain in your own words when you would prefer each and what safety difference you noticed.
rubric: states both produce the same result
gives a reason grounded in readability or intent
mentions that at() is bounds-checked while [] is not

exercises.title: The base is never constructed
exercises.prompt: This program does not compile. Read the error, then fix it so that the base class is constructed properly.

exercises.title: Two copies too many
exercises.prompt: This operator copies the object twice and cannot be used on a const object. Fix it.

exercises.title: Static or dynamic?
exercises.prompt: Predict what this prints, and say which call is resolved at run time.
